opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic reason is that software engineering isn't as special as it looks. It's the domain where progress has been fastest because it has unusually good properties for training: you can run the code, you can write tests, you get a lot of fairly cheap, fairly reliable feedback. But the underlying skills the models are picking up — breaking a problem into pieces, keeping track of a long chain of reasoning, noticing when something has gone wrong and backing up — are general skills. They aren't specific to Python.

So the question is really whether other domains can be made to look enough like software engineering from a training perspective. And I think for a lot of them the answer is yes, at least partially. Mathematics is the obvious next case, because you have formal verification and proof checkers, so you get the same kind of crisp signal. A lot of science has pieces like that too: you can check whether a calculation is right, whether a simulation reproduces known results, whether a prediction holds up. Even in messier domains, a surprising fraction of the work decomposes into subtasks that are checkable, and the models are getting better at doing that decomposition themselves.

The other piece is that software is itself a lever on everything else. Once a model is a very good engineer, it can build its own tools, run its own experiments, write its own evaluation harnesses. A lot of research in, say, biology or materials science is bottlenecked on exactly that kind of engineering work. So even if the model's raw judgment in a field lags, the engineering capability spills over.

Where I'd be more cautious is the fuzzier tasks, where there's no good ground truth: strategy, policy judgment, a lot of what we care about in alignment research itself. There you're relying on human feedback or on models judging models, and that's much harder to make reliable. That's a big part of why I work on things like debate and scalable oversight. I don't think capabilities will stall at that boundary, but I do think it's where things are most likely to go wrong in subtle ways, because the models can get good at seeming right before they get good at being right.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the reason I find software engineering interesting as a reference point is that it's the domain where we've seen the clearest, fastest progress, and I think it's worth asking why that is rather than treating it as some special exception. Code is a domain where you get lots of fast, cheap feedback. You can run the tests, you can see whether the thing compiles, you can check whether the output matches. So it's very natural to set up a training loop where the model tries something, gets a signal, and improves. That's a big part of why we've seen models go from barely completing a function to doing multi-hour engineering tasks in a few years.

Now, the question is whether that structure is unique to code, and I don't think it is. A lot of tasks that look very different from software engineering on the surface actually have the same shape underneath. Mathematics is the obvious one, where you can check proofs formally or at least check answers. But even in messier areas like scientific research, a lot of the work decomposes into subtasks where you can tell whether you succeeded. Did the experiment reproduce? Does the analysis match the data? Does the argument hold up when someone pushes on it? The feedback is slower and noisier than running a unit test, but it exists.

The other thing I'd say is that the skills transfer more than people expect. When you train a model to be good at long-horizon engineering work, it's not just learning syntax. It's learning to plan, to break down a problem, to notice when it's confused, to go back and check, to use tools, to keep track of a lot of context over a long period. Those are fairly general capabilities, and we see them showing up in domains the model wasn't specifically trained on.

And then there's a third path, which is that software engineering itself is a lever on everything else. If you have a model that can build tools, set up evaluations, and automate the process of generating feedback in a new domain, then it can help construct the training environments that get you capability in that domain. So I think of software engineering less as the ceiling and more as the first rung, and the thing that lets you reach the next ones.

That said, I want to be a bit careful. There are domains where feedback is genuinely scarce or where the ground truth is contested, and I think progress there will be slower and harder to measure. I'm not claiming it's all going to fall at once. But the argument that there's something magic about code that doesn't generalise, I find that fairly weak, and most of the evidence we've accumulated points the other way.

astra-6.text:
I think software engineering is an especially convenient place to train these systems, because you can try something and get feedback: you can run the code, run tests, and see whether it works. But that feedback loop isn’t unique to software engineering.

In mathematics, you can check proofs. In other domains, you can make predictions and compare them with observations, or propose experiments and look at the results. The feedback may be slower or more expensive, and that matters a lot. But there’s a plausible path from learning to solve problems where checking is cheap to solving problems where checking requires more work.

There’s also the question of transfer. Writing software involves breaking a problem into pieces, forming hypotheses, testing them, and revising your approach when something fails. Those are useful abilities outside programming. We shouldn’t assume that transfer will happen automatically, but I don’t see a strong reason to expect those abilities to stop being useful at the boundary of software engineering.

sol-6.1.text:
I think software engineering is a particularly convenient place to start because you can check a lot of the work. You can run the code, run tests, and get feedback about whether the model has succeeded. That makes it easier to train on increasingly difficult tasks. But I don’t think the capabilities you develop that way are exclusively about software. Breaking a problem down, forming a hypothesis, testing it, noticing that it failed, and trying something else are useful in many domains.

The question is how you get good feedback in those other domains. In mathematics you have proofs; in science you have experiments. In other cases the feedback is slower or harder to interpret, and that could make progress substantially harder. But there’s a plausible path where models use tools, interact with an environment, and learn from the results, rather than just producing an answer in one shot.

So I wouldn’t take success at coding as a guarantee of success everywhere. But I also wouldn’t expect a sharp boundary where the ability to reason through complicated problems suddenly stops being useful because the output isn’t code.
